## Abstract

There is **no on-site class this week**. Instead, use this decentralized working
week to lay the groundwork for the country-analysis project you will pursue over
the semester. Two things need to happen:

- **Form your groups and settle on a country group.** Talk to each other, team up,
  and start thinking about which group of countries you want to work on.
- **Read your reading group's entry text into Ecological Economics.** Each text opens
  the field from a different angle. We will discuss them together next week, so come
  prepared.

## Group formation and country selection

Get together with your fellow students and **form your project groups yourselves**.
Start discussing which **country group** you would like to analyse — this early
conversation is what the week is for.

You can organise this among yourselves, and you are welcome to use the
**Group Formation tool** in our
[Moodle room (17919)](https://elearning.uni-flensburg.de/moodle/course/view.php?id=17919)
to find and join a group.

::: {.callout-important}
## Deadline: groups fixed by the third week

Your groups must be **fixed by the third week (30.09.)**. The groups entered in the
Moodle Group Formation tool at that point are **final**, and **every group must be
registered there** — a group that is not in the Moodle tool does not count. Please
make sure your whole group is entered before we meet again.
:::

## Foundational readings: entry texts into Ecological Economics

Take the time this week to read **one entry text** into Ecological Economics. Each text
opens the field from a different angle, and we will discuss all of them together next
week — so come prepared to report on yours.

We split the course into **reading groups**, one text per group. How many groups there
are depends on the size of the course: normally **three**, with a **fourth** added only
if the course is large enough to need it. The assignment of reading groups will be
announced in Session 1; note that these reading groups are **not** the same as your
country-analysis project groups.

The texts are:

- **Text 1 (Reading group 1):** @common2005 — *Ecological Economics: An Introduction*.
- **Text 2 (Reading group 2):** @spash2018 — *Social Ecological Economics*.
- **Text 3 (Reading group 3):** @martinezalier2015 — *Taking Stock: The Keystones of
  Ecological Economics*.
- **Text 4 (Reading group 4):** announced in Session 1 — this text is only used if the
  course is large enough to need a fourth group.

You may read and discuss the text within your group, but you do not have to — reading
it individually is perfectly fine.

### Prepare this general question

For the discussion, come ready to answer — in **one sentence**:

> In one sentence, what was the most surprising or challenging idea your text presented?

### Guiding questions for the texts

Use the following guiding questions to focus your reading. They are organised around
three themes; for each theme, compare what your text argues with the contrasting
position.

#### What does need change?

- **Reading group 1 (Common & Stagl):** Your text talks about making the economy
  "sustainable" — what specific changes does that imply?
- **Reading group 2 (Spash):** Your text calls for "radical transformation" — what does that
  mean concretely, versus what Common & Stagl suggest?

#### How should the environment be measured?

- **Reading group 2 (Spash):** Your text critiques putting monetary values on ecosystem
  services. What's wrong with calculating "the value of nature"?
- **Reading group 1 (Common & Stagl):** Your text is more open to multiple methods — where
  does monetary valuation fit appropriately?

#### Who is in power to shape environmental policy?

- **Reading group 2 (Spash):** Your text emphasises corporations, technology lock-in, and
  imperial modes of living. How visible is this in mainstream environmental policy?
- **Reading group 1 (Common & Stagl):** Your text is more about analytical frameworks. Do
  these frameworks have politics hidden in them?

::: {.callout-tip}
## Connect it to your project

For every one of these questions, also ask yourself: **What, if anything, do you take
from this for your country analysis?**
